title: Getting Started
summary: Install Mosaic and configure one channel before creating a song.
prose:
Mosaic is a rhythm and harmony sequencer for norns and a 128 grid. It combines Elektron-style pattern editing and parameter locks with generative patterns and modulation. Use it to build patterns and arrange them into a song, playing MIDI instruments or internal norns sound sources.

Patterns supply trigs, relative notes and velocities. Channels assign these patterns to outputs and add exceptions. Scale slots define harmony. Song slots store sections.

Four words recur in the examples. A trig is an active step, a point where a note can sound. A mask is a note, velocity, length or trig value set on a channel or on one step, and it overrides the pattern's value. A merge combines the patterns assigned to one channel. A lock stores a parameter value on one step.

Follow [Make a piece](#learn) to keep one project from four equal notes to a saved two-section arrangement. Begin with [Choose one sound](#setup), then [Make four notes](#first-sound). Each chapter states its incoming project, action and result.

The interactive examples below preview ideas that later chapters teach, and each one states its own starting point. The one to follow now is "Create a four-step loop from an empty project". Come back to the others when you reach masks, scales, channel settings and the composition workflow.

Use [No Sound](#no-sound) if the playhead moves without audible output. Open the Reference when you need a particular parameter rather than continuing the course.

title: Installing Mosaic
summary: Install Mosaic from maiden or the norns community catalogue.
prose:
1. In maiden, enter `;install https://github.com/subvertnormality/mosaic`, or install Mosaic from the norns community catalogue.
2. Connect a 128 grid.
3. Select Mosaic from the norns script list.
4. Continue with [Setup](#setup).

When replacing an alpha or beta installation, back up your projects and custom configurations first. Then remove the old installation and its `data/mosaic` folder before installing Mosaic 1.4.0. This applies only to that migration, not to a routine reinstallation.

title: Configuring an Output
summary: Route channel 1 to one instrument.
prose:
Before starting: Mosaic is installed, a grid is connected and a new project is stopped. Record is off. Choose either a working MIDI instrument or an enabled Polyperc 1 player.

Settings in this chapter belong to one channel at a time. Select a channel with its button in the top row of the grid. The header (CH01, CH02) names the channel the screen is editing. Another channel keeps its own device, MIDI port, MIDI channel and clock until you select it and change it. The first example below shows channel 1 and channel 2 holding different settings.

### Open Device

1. Tap Channel (3,8).
2. Check CH01.
3. Turn E1 to Channel tasks.
4. Select Device with E2 and press K3.

Device opens for channel 1.

### Apply one output

1. Select a working MIDI output or enabled Polyperc 1 with E3. For a MIDI instrument that has no configuration file, choose CC Device, Mosaic's built-in generic MIDI device. It plays notes and offers CC 1 to 127 as parameters. Choose a stock or custom configuration instead when one matches your instrument.
2. For MIDI, select port and channel with E2 and adjust each with E3 to match the receiver.
3. Press K3 to apply.

The selected output becomes active. Selecting a draft alone does not apply it.

### Set the tempo

1. Tap Song (6,8).
2. Turn E1 to Song tasks; select Tempo & feel with E2 and press K3.
3. Select Tempo with E2; set 90 BPM with E3.
4. Press K3 to apply.
5. Return to Channel (3,8).

The project uses 90 BPM. At the default Rate /1 (sixteenth notes), each channel step lasts one sixth of a second. Rate is a channel setting: Channel tasks → Clock.

Resulting project: CH01 routes to a working MIDI instrument or Polyperc 1; no pattern assigned.

details.title: Recovery
details.text: Check the destination port/channel or enabled player before changing notes.

details.title: Course continuity
details.text: Continue the same project through Make a piece. The separate reference demonstrations below start from their stated starting projects; they do not load a replacement into your project.

title: Hardware Requirements
summary: Mosaic requires norns and a 128 grid.
prose:
Connect a 128 grid to norns. For internal sound, install a supported n.b. player and use the norns audio output. For external sound, connect a MIDI instrument and configure its receiving channel.

A MIDI keyboard is optional. It can enter notes into held steps or record into a playing channel. Crow, Just Friends and Ansible require their supported n.b. integrations and the corresponding hardware.

Any device with MIDI in works as a generic CC Device. A stock or custom device configuration gives it named parameters and defaults and is the best-supported option. For an ACL Sinfonion, a hardware build keeps Mosaic's quantiser in sync with the Eurorack module (see Sinfonion Connect).

A MIDI controller whose encoders send relative (binary offset) values makes data entry easier: it can be mapped to channel parameters (see MIDI controller mapping). The keyboard and the controller are separate roles; one device can serve as both.

title: MIDI Device Configuration
summary: Device configurations define output defaults and mapped parameters.
prose:
A device configuration supplies parameter names, CC/NRPN assignments and output defaults. Basic MIDI note output does not require a custom configuration.

1. Put the required JSON device files in `data/mosaic/config`.
2. Restart Mosaic to discover the files.
3. Open Channel tasks → Device.
4. Select the device and press K3 to apply.
5. Check the MIDI port and channel against the receiving instrument.

Use a [stock configuration](#stock-devices), or [create a custom configuration](#adding-custom-devices) from the instrument’s MIDI implementation.

After a configured device is applied, its parameters appear in the norns PARAMS menu under MOSAIC, in that channel's device parameters, and can be assigned to trig parameter slots. Each parameter holds a value from its minimum to its maximum, or X for Off. X sends no value and leaves the instrument's own setting alone. The example below uses a example MIDI device with a parameter named Control 1 (CC 1) to show the value range, clamping at both ends and the Off position.

title: Installing Stock Device Configurations
summary: Copy selected stock JSON files into data/mosaic/config.
prose:
1. In maiden, open `code/mosaic/lib/config`. Digitone, Digitakt 2, Syntakt and Nord Drum 2 have fully tailored mappings. The folder also holds further maps, including Digitakt, Vermona DRM voices, OP-1, Plaits, Braids and MIDI SID.
2. Create `data/mosaic/config` if it does not exist.
3. Copy the required JSON files into that folder.
4. Restart Mosaic.
5. Open Channel tasks → Device, select the map and press K3. The device becomes available to the channel.

Check its MIDI output port and channel. The receiving instrument must use the matching setup.

Only the files you copy become devices, so the Device list holds just your own instruments. Once a configured device is applied, its parameters behave as in the example below: Control 1 sends CC 1 from 0 to 127, and X means Off.

title: Creating a Custom Device Configuration
summary: Create a JSON map from the instrument’s MIDI implementation.
prose:
1. Open the [Mosaic Config Creator](https://subvertnormality.github.io/mosaic/config_creator.html).

2. Enter the instrument’s port, MIDI channel, note policy and CC/NRPN addresses.

3. Save the JSON file in `data/mosaic/config`.

4. Restart Mosaic.

5. Select the device in Channel tasks → Device and press K3.

Invalid configurations are skipped so valid devices can still load. Mosaic reads configurations from `data/mosaic/config`. Ignore any older instruction that names a `dust > mosaic > config` folder.

You can also copy a stock configuration into `data/mosaic/config` and edit it, for example to set the default MIDI output device. Without any configuration a MIDI channel can still use CC Device: it plays notes and offers CC 1 to 127, and you look up the CC numbers yourself.

The example below shows what a configured parameter does once its device is applied: Control 1 sends CC 1 from 0 to 127, and X means Off.

title: Lock lead time
summary: Set the lead time for MIDI parameter locks before their step.
prose:
Some synths smooth incoming CC values. A filter or level change sent at the same moment as a note then arrives late and glides through the start of the note. Lock lead time sends each step's lock values slightly before the step so they have settled when the note sounds. The notes themselves keep their timing.

1. Tap K1 briefly and open the norns PARAMS menu.
2. Open MOSAIC and select **Lock lead time (ms)** in the Parameter locks section.
3. Turn E3 to set the required lead time. The menu displays the selected value.
4. Return to Mosaic to compare playback.

Worked values at 130 BPM, where one clock pulse lasts about 4.8 ms. A lead of 0 sends each lock value with its note. A lead of 25 sends it about 28.8 ms ahead (6 pulses). A lead of 50 sends it about 52.9 ms ahead (11 pulses). Listen for the filter or parameter change landing before the note starts instead of sweeping through its attack.
This global setting accepts 0–50 ms and defaults to **25 ms**. It gives MIDI CC/NRPN
parameter locks time to settle before the note attack, particularly on devices
that smooth incoming controllers. Set it to **0** to send each value at its own
step, which is the original output timing. The value is saved with Mosaic's
project settings.

A step's parameter values leave ahead of the step, in an earlier clock pulse.
Nothing is delayed to achieve this: note-ons, note-offs, live MIDI-thru, outgoing
MIDI Clock, Start, Continue, Stop and song position all keep the timing they have
at a lead of 0, and gate lengths are unchanged. N.b. players are unaffected.

Because a value leaves on a clock pulse, the wait it achieves is the setting
rounded **up** to the next whole pulse, so a value never leaves with less lead
than was asked for. At 130 bpm a pulse is about 4.8 ms, so a 25 ms setting
delivers about 28.8 ms; at 200 bpm it delivers 25 ms exactly. The figure follows
the tempo, and every value of a step leaves on the same pulse, so what you hear
stays consistent between events rather than fixed to the number in the menu.

No step is looked ahead musically: probability, conditions, fills, random notes,
strum, arps and micro-timing still make their decisions at their own times. Only
the parameter values a step will send are resolved early.

Every note sounds with its own step's values. When two notes on the same MIDI
channel are less than twice the lead apart (a fast tempo, a fast channel clock,
or swing and shuffle bringing steps together), a value does not take the whole
lead: it waits until halfway between the previous sounding note and its own step.
The previous note keeps its value through the first half of the gap, and the new
value settles in the second half. A trigless step sounds nothing, so it is not
the note a later value waits behind. A strummed chord's later voices are sounding
notes, so the next step's values wait behind the last of them.

An address that more than one slot writes, whether two slots of one channel or
two channels addressing one device parameter, is not sent early: its values leave
at their own step, in the order the step would send them at a lead of 0.

Two cases give no lead at all. The first step after Play resolves its lock on the
transport's own first pulse, so there is no earlier pulse for its values to leave
in and they leave with the note. A parameter that is mid-slide keeps its slide
until the slide's destination step, so that step's lock arrives with the step
rather than before it. Nothing is delayed to hide either case.

The lead covers the time a receiver takes for a parameter change to take effect,
so every value follows the same rule whether or not its step has a note: trigless
locks, assigned values and slide values leave ahead of the step they belong to and
take effect as that step is heard.

Editing a lock that has already left changes what the next pass sends, and the
edited value is sent again at its own step, so the receiver is corrected rather
than left holding the superseded value. Stopping playback or using Panic releases held voices and clears pending parameter-lock output.

title: Selecting an n.b. Player
summary: Install and enable a supported player before assigning it to a channel.
prose:
1. Install the player’s n.b. mod.
2. Enable the mod in the norns MODS menu and restart as required by the mod.
3. Start Mosaic.
4. Open Channel tasks → Device. Turn E3 to the player. The row shows its name as a draft. Press K3 to apply it.

Supported, enabled players appear in the Device list. A mod that is installed but not on Mosaic's list of supported players does not appear. Mosaic supports Doubledecker, Oilcan, Polyperc and Emplaitress as n.b. players. Sound examples use Doubledecker, Oilcan and Polyperc. Emplaitress requires MiPlaits to be installed and enabled. Availability depends on the installed player and its dependencies. Crow, Just Friends and Ansible also require their corresponding hardware.

A channel has one device, so give each player its own channel. The audio example Rhythm, bass and a changing chord assigns Oilcan 1 (percussion) to channel 1, Polyperc 1 (bass) to channel 2 and Doubledecker (chords) to channel 3. To apply a player, press K3 when the confirmation prompt appears. Reopen Channel tasks → Device to confirm that the selected player remains assigned. Listen to the audio example to hear what the three players sound like together.

Do not overload norns with too many internal sound engines on different channels.

title: MIDI Keyboard Input
summary: Hold a step to enter it, or arm recording and play.
prose:
To audition the selected channel without recording:

1. Select the channel and apply its output device.
2. Leave Record disarmed and release all grid steps.
3. Play and release MIDI keys. The channel’s selected output plays the notes; no step masks are entered.

To enter a step:

1. Select the destination channel.
2. Hold the destination channel step.
3. Play a MIDI note or chord. On the Masks screen the entered values appear as locks on the held step.
4. Release the MIDI keys, then release the grid step.
5. Set the note length manually.

For live entry, arm Record `(2,8)` and play during playback. Notes are assigned to the active step when processed. A recorded chord shares one length from its first key press to its final release.

By default, MIDI input plays the pressed keys. Map scale to white keys maps the selected scale onto white keys with its root at C. The scale-degree and rotation options affect this mapping.

### Map scale to white keys

With the option on, the white keys play the selected scale from its root on C, one scale note per white key. Keys C D E F G A B C play:

- C major: 60, 62, 64, 65, 67, 69, 71, 72.
- Natural minor from C: 60, 62, 63, 65, 67, 68, 70, 72.

A black key plays the same pitch as the white key above it. With the option off, every key plays its own pitch whatever the scale. The example below turns the option on in C major, changes the scale to natural minor, then turns it off.

### Channel and step masks

Keyboard entry writes masks. A mask replaces the pattern's value for that channel or step: Note, Vel (velocity), Len (length) and Trig. A channel mask applies to every step. A step mask, set while the step is held, overrides the channel mask. X means no mask is set, so the pattern's value is used. Velocity 0 is silent and is different from X. Hold a step and press K2 to clear that step's masks. The two Masks examples below show channel masks, step masks and clearing.

title: MIDI Controller Mapping
summary: Assign MIDI controls to channel parameters through the norns MIDI Map menu.
prose:
Use a MIDI controller that supports relative (binary offset) messages.

1. Open the norns PARAMS menu and select Mosaic Midi Mapping.
2. Choose selected channel parameters for the currently selected channel, or channel parameters for a fixed channel. Select the required parameter.
3. Hold K1 and press K3 to switch from EDIT to MAP mode.
4. Press K3 to open the parameter’s map editor. Select Learn and press K3 to arm it.
5. Operate the MIDI control. The editor learns its CC, input channel and device.
6. Set Input low to 1, Input high to 2 and Accum to Yes. Check that Output low is −1.0 and Output high is 1.0, and set them if not. Use E2 to select a row and E3 to change it.
7. Press K2 to leave the editor and save the assignment.
8. Hold K1 and press K3 to return to EDIT mode, then leave the parameter menu.
9. Operate the mapped MIDI control. The selected Mosaic value changes.

Trig parameters, masks and channel memory can be mapped. The first MIDI message used by Learn identifies the control; it does not perform the mapped parameter change.

### How relative messages change a value

A relative (binary offset) control sends 64 for no change. A value above 64 means up and a value below 64 means down. In the examples, 65 is one step up and 63 is one step down, and 0 is also a decrease. The settings above (Input 1 to 2, Accum Yes) make each message move the mapped value one step and add up. Messages that arrive quickly one after another move it further.

A value that can be Off starts at X, one step below 0. The first increase from X reaches 0. A velocity mask at X, sent eleven messages of 65, reads 10. Two messages of 63 then bring it to 8.

### Selected and fixed channel maps

A selected-channel map edits whichever channel is selected when you turn the control. A fixed-channel map always edits its own channel. The first example below maps CC 20 to the selected channel's velocity mask and CC 21 to channel 2's, and shows both. The second example builds the CC 20 map in the norns menu and then uses it.

[MIDI controller mapping demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iGx5fmrbatA&t=802s)

title: Controls and Navigation
summary: Use the bottom-row page keys and check the screen header.
prose:
Mosaic is played on the grid and read on the norns screen. Grid coordinates are `(column,row)`, counted from the top left. The bottom-left keys are Play `(1,8)`, Record `(2,8)`, Channel `(3,8)`, Scale `(4,8)`, Pattern `(5,8)` and Song `(6,8)`.

1. Press the required page key. The screen shows that page.
2. Check the header. `CH01` identifies channel 1; `ST05` identifies held step 5.
3. Release a held step to return to channel scope.

When a procedure says hold, keep the control pressed until the release instruction.

The examples below each show one editor. Choose a trig algorithm is in the Pattern editor, Prepare a scale before applying it is in the Scale editor, Set the global song length is in the Song editor and Keep each channel independent is in the Channel editor. Their starting points are stated above each example.

title: Starting and Stopping Playback
summary: Grid (1,8) starts and stops the sequencer.
prose:
1. Press Grid `(1,8)` to start. The grid playhead advances through the sequence.
2. Press Grid `(1,8)` again to stop.

With Shift press stop enabled, stop with a long press or hold K1 while pressing Grid `(1,8)`. Panic releases hanging voices without stopping the sequencer; use Grid `(1,8)` to stop playback.

[Start and stop demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J1ckUZvhFJ0&t=632s)

title: Arm live record
summary: Record notes and edited parameters into the selected channel.
prose:
1. Select the channel and apply its output.
2. Tap Record `(2,8)` to arm recording.
3. Start playback and play notes on the MIDI keyboard. Notes become masks on the selected channel at the step active when Mosaic processes each note-on.
4. Release the keys to finish the recorded note lengths. A chord shares one length from its first press to its final release, quantised to the nearest supported note length.
5. Tap Record again to disarm. Notes already begun while armed retain their lengths when released.

To record a trig parameter, edit its value while recording is armed. Mosaic records that value on subsequent eligible steps; earlier steps are unchanged. With Trigless Locks on, every step is eligible. With it off, only active steps are eligible. Stop or disarm clears pending parameter recording.

Selecting another channel or Scale pauses pending parameter recording; returning can resume it. Read the parameter-recording rules before changing assignments or using slides during a take.

### Record a short phrase from a keyboard

1. Select the channel, apply its output and assign a pattern over the steps it should loop. A four-step range is enough.
2. If an external MIDI clock drives the sequencer, set the norns clock Source to midi first (PARAMS → CLOCK) and start the external clock.
3. Tap Record (2,8) to arm.
4. Play notes on the keyboard while the sequencer runs. Each note-on becomes a note mask on the step that is playing, with the velocity you played. The recorded steps light on the grid.
5. Tap Record again to disarm. Notes still held keep their lengths when you release them.
6. To run Mosaic on its own clock, set Source back to internal and the tempo you want, then tap Play (1,8). The recorded steps repeat with the spacing you played.

The example below plays note 72 at velocity 90 and note 79 at velocity 80 under a 100 BPM external clock. They land on steps 2 and 4. At the default Rate /1 and 90 BPM they replay one third of a second apart.

details.title: Parameter recording interactions
details.text:
To enable record mode, press the second button from the left on the grid.

When record mode is active, any notes played on a MIDI keyboard will be captured as note masks on the currently selected channel. This includes note lengths and chords. All recordings are quantised to align with the current step: the step active when Mosaic processes the note-on, rather than the nearest step. An incoming MIDI clock pulse and a sequencer step transition are separate events; a note processed before the transition still belongs to the preceding active step. A recorded chord has one shared note length, measured from the first key press to the final key release and quantised to the nearest supported note length. This applies even when the chord keys are pressed or released at different times. Disarming recording prevents new notes from being recorded. Notes that began while recording was armed are kept, and their full note lengths are measured and committed when you release them, even if recording has since been disarmed.

While recording is armed, editing a trig parameter starts recording that parameter’s value on subsequent eligible steps processed for the selected channel. Already-processed steps are unchanged. Only edited parameters are recorded, overwriting their existing locks through the channel’s final step; recording clears before its next starting step is processed while the channel remains selected. Further encoder edits update or restart recording. Grid Stop or disarm clears pending parameter recording. Active MIDI values are sent again before each eligible step’s note, even when the value has not changed. Selecting another channel or the Scale Editor pauses this parameter recording; returning resumes on the next eligible step unless that step clears recording at the selected channel’s wrap. Wraps while the channel is not selected leave its pending values intact. An active recorded value cancels that slot’s existing slide at the next eligible step. Off sends nothing and leaves an existing slide running. Changing a parameter assignment clears its pending recording; confirming the same assignment preserves it. Applying a MIDI device, channel or port change resets the device locks, assignments, defaults and pending parameter recording. Unconfirmed changes and cancellation leave the original recording intact.

With Trigless Locks off, parameter values are recorded only on active steps. When it is on, every step is eligible. Trigless Locks is enabled by default.

title: Selecting a Grid Page
summary: Grid (3,8) through (6,8) select the four editors.
prose:
Press Grid `(3,8)` for Channel, `(4,8)` for Scale, `(5,8)` for Pattern or `(6,8)` for Song. The norns screen follows the selected page, and selecting a channel on the Channel page shows that channel on the screen.

Press Pattern repeatedly to cycle Trig → Note → Velocity. Channels hold output settings and masks. Patterns hold source material. Scales hold pitch collections. Song slots hold variations of the sequence.

Press and hold one or more channel steps to edit exactly those steps on their own. The screen shows the step's Masks and the header reads the step, for example `CH03 ST05`. Release the step and the screen returns to the page you were on. The example below taps through the page keys, holds step 5 and then holds step 9 from the Clock page.

recipes.title: Return from a held-step edit to the page you were using
recipes.text:
Purpose: this recorded check distinguishes the temporary held-step Masks header from the Clock page that returns on release. It also shows that a local C-2 exception does not change channel Note X. See [Inspect a step and return](#grid-menu-navigation/hold-step-return) for the captured headers and local result.

Starting point: Playback is stopped, channel 3 is selected, and Channel tasks > Clock is open. No step is held; channel Note is X.

1. Hold step 9 at grid (9,4). The screen temporarily shows NOTE MASKS CH03 ST09. Release step 9. The Clock page returns.

2. Hold step 5 at grid (5,4). The screen shows NOTE MASKS CH03 ST05. Turn E2 anticlockwise until Note is selected, then turn E3 clockwise one detent. Step 5 changes from X to C-2 (MIDI 0). A Note mask alone does not create a trig.

3. Release step 5. The Clock page returns. Open Channel tasks > Masks and confirm channel 3 Note still reads X; the C-2 exception belongs only to step 5. Return to Clock if you want to leave the example as you found it.

Outcome: Holding and releasing step 9 while Clock is open temporarily shows Masks and restores Clock. The separate step-5 edit remains local to that step, while the channel Note default remains X.

title: Norns Menu Navigation
summary: Open tasks with E1; choose a row with E2 and change its value with E3.
prose:
1. Turn E1 to open the current context’s task list.
2. Select a task with E1 or E2.
3. Press K3 to open it.
4. Turn E2 to choose a vertical row.
5. Turn E3 to change the selected value.

Long values appear on a separate full-width line. A position indicator identifies the selected row when the list extends beyond the screen. The header retains the current page and channel or pattern scope.

For staged Device, Clock, Scale and Song settings, press K3 to apply; K2 cancels the draft or returns to its parent. For a row marked OPEN >, K3 opens the nested list. Check the footer for the selected row’s action.

Masks keep eight controls visible together on one screen. Masks and Trig params update their values directly. Their held-step K2 clear operation and K1 combinations remain as described on those pages; they are not cancelled drafts. Hold a channel step to edit its local values, then release to return to channel scope.

A short K1 tap opens the norns system menu. Holding K1 is Shift. E1 opens task lists. Hold K1 while turning E3 for fine changes where a value supports them.

Most of the time you play the grid and glance at the screen; you only navigate the screen to reach settings. Hold one or more steps and the Channel screen shows the masks or the trig params, whichever page you were on, for exactly those steps; release to return.

The first example below keeps channel settings per channel. The second opens Channel tasks, scrolls the list and opens History and Device.

details.title: Reading the screen
details.text:
The title row names the screen and its scope. `CH03` is the channel. `S02` is the song slot when it is not the first. `ST05` is one held step and `3ST` is several held steps. `PAT02 CH01` is the pattern editor showing pattern 2 over channel 1. A Channel screen also shows `MUTE` when the channel is muted, `OCT+1` when its octave is not 0 and `O-1` for a held step's octave lock.

The selected field is outlined or marked with `>`, and its whole value is always shown. On a grid of fields the value sits in its cell. When a cell is too narrow it shows `...` and the full value appears on the last line next to the field's name. A single-field screen shows the value in large type. Screens change instantly, without a transition.

The four small tiles at the right of the title row are Mosaic's mark; they light up in turn when something changes.

details.title: Screens that open themselves
details.text:
A grid action opens the screen that shows what it changed, with that value selected. A merge button or a pattern assignment shows Merge modes, where E2 and E3 also change the trig, note, velocity and length merge modes. A channel scale lock shows Scale source. Global transposition and scale-track locks show Scale overview. The song length fader shows Song playback. Press K2 or turn E1 to carry on from there.

Screens that only show information, such as Scale overview, Song playback and Paint preview, list every value at once with no cursor.

details.title: Task lists
details.text:
E1 opens the task list for the page you are on, and the list opens on the row of the screen you came from. Each detent of E1 or E2 moves one row, and the list stops at its first and last rows. Press K3 to open the highlighted task.

Channel tasks: Masks, Trig params, Output, Clock, Merge modes, Merge Shape, Harmony, Device and History. Scale tasks: Scale, Scale clock and Overview. Pattern tasks: Pattern, Options, Algorithm, Channel view and, while the Rhythm Doctor algorithm is chosen, Rhythm Doctor. Song tasks: Playback, Slot setup, Tempo and feel and Channel view.

Other settings are in the norns PARAMS menu under MOSAIC: projects, sequencer options, MIDI mapping and each channel's device parameters. A short K1 tap opens it. The Channel tasks footer reminds you with `K1 PARAMS`.

details.title: Staged changes
details.text: Device, clock, scale and song settings show your change straight away but apply only when you press K3. K2, or leaving the screen with E1, cancels a staged change without touching what is playing. Merge Shape and Harmony keep a whole draft in the same way.

details.title: Start-up animation
details.text: When Mosaic starts, the logo's dots and bars lay down across the screen row by row, lift away to leave the mosaic wordmark, and fade into the first screen. Any key, encoder or grid press skips it. UI Motion turns the animation and the movement of the screen characters off. For the layout of the norns itself, see the [norns documentation](https://monome.org/docs/norns/).

title: Tooltips
summary: The screen footer displays controls or feedback for the last grid action.
prose:
Perform a grid action to show its tooltip in the screen footer. The footer otherwise lists available controls.

Check the header and selected value before editing. The header identifies the channel and any held-step scope.

In the Pattern editor, tapping Prime, Cancel or a Move button also shows the Paint Preview screen, which reports whether a preview is showing, its algorithm, its shift and how many steps it triggers. The example below uses these controls.

title: External MIDI Transport
summary: An external MIDI clock can drive the transport.
prose:
To follow an external clock:

1. Open the norns PARAMS menu with a short K1 tap and open the CLOCK group.
2. Turn E3 on Source to midi. Mosaic now follows the clock, Start and Stop it receives, and its tempo follows the sender's.
3. To return to Mosaic's own clock, turn Source back to internal and set the tempo you want on the tempo row.

The example below does this with a sender running at 100 BPM and ends by setting the tempo back to 90.

With the norns clock source set to MIDI, external MIDI Clock drives Mosaic at 24 pulses per quarter note. Norns receives clock from all connected MIDI devices by default; use **CLOCK > midi clock in** to select one input when other devices also send transport or clock. Mosaic follows received pulse order: a missing pulse delays later step boundaries and an extra pulse advances them; norns estimates timing between received pulses from recent intervals. If clock pulses disappear without Stop, norns continues at its last acquired tempo and does not infer Stop. A later external Start marks the next Clock as beat zero. When that Clock arrives, Mosaic releases held notes and resets to step 1, including when it is already playing. Restart cleanup does not send a MIDI Stop back to connected devices; an ordinary Stop still releases notes and sends Stop. The grid Play button starts Mosaic locally at the current clock phase.

Mosaic does not interpret MIDI Continue or Song Position Pointer as clock-transport commands. When either arrives, playback remains stopped at its current position. Send MIDI Start to begin again from step 1. Scripts can still receive both messages through the MIDI event API.

title: MIDI Panic
summary: Send a Note Off sweep without stopping the sequencer.
prose:
Use Panic when a MIDI device holds a note that will not stop.

1. If new notes must not follow, stop playback with Play/Stop (1,8). This is optional; Panic does not stop the sequencer.
2. Hold the navigation button of a page you are not on for about a second. For example, with Song showing, hold Channel (3,8).
3. Release the button after the Note Off sweep. The selected page does not change.

Panic sends Note Off for every note on every MIDI channel and connected device. Holding the selected page button does not trigger Panic.

Panic does not stop the sequencer or cancel scheduled strum or arpeggio voices. Playback and scheduled voices continue, so new notes can sound during or after the sweep. Use Play/Stop to stop playback.

details.title: Panic and connected devices
details.text: After Panic sends its Note Off sweep, the connected instrument determines how quickly its sound releases. Use Play/Stop separately to stop playback; Panic does not stop the sequencer or cancel scheduled strum and arpeggio voices.

details.title: Independent controls example: C-C-C-D over a bass
details.text:
Before starting: Start with stopped channel 1 assigned pattern 1, range 16, attacks 1,5,9,13, channel Note 60/Vel 80/Len 1/2 and step 13 Note 62/Vel 50. A second channel can use pattern 2 with attacks 1,9, relative degrees 0,4 and octave −1. Apply C major. [Make a piece](#learn) chapters 2–6 give the full preparation. If using only one channel, ignore the bass comparison.

Harmony can apply globally, moving every channel to the same key, degree and rotation, or per channel. Because patterns store relative notes, you can change the global scale on a different cycle from a the channel note data for polyrhythmic tonal movement. A project has 16 scale slots, each with a root, scale type, degree, transposition and rotation. Sequence them with Scale locks, globally from the Scale editor or per channel in the Channel editor. See [Scale editor](#scale-editor) and [Scale locks](#scale-locks).

### Restore note inheritance

1. Select CH01 and open Masks.
2. With no step held, set Note to X.
3. Hold step 13 and press K2, then release.
4. Select Vel, hold step 13, set 50 and release.

All Note exceptions are cleared. K2 also cleared the velocity exception, which is deliberately restored.

### Retain the same melody in the pattern

1. Tap Pattern (5,8) until Note is shown; select pattern 1 at (1,1).
2. Tap (1,7), (5,7) and (9,7) for degree 0.
3. Tap (13,6) for degree 1.
4. Play two bars and stop.

C–C–C–D returns through relative notes. The quieter ending stays in the channel mask.

### Prepare a second scale

1. Open Scale (4,8).
2. Select scale slot 2.
3. Play two bars and stop to hear its stored C-major setting.
4. Select Root with E2; set D with E3.
5. Select Scale and choose Major.

The melody and bass still use C major during the comparison. D major is now prepared in the draft; press K3 before using the grid.

### Compare the transposition

1. Press K3 to apply D major.
2. Play two bars and stop.
3. Select the unchanged C-major slot 1 and press K3.

The phrase becomes D–D–D–E and bass D–A. Rhythm and velocity are preserved. C major is restored for the arrangement.

Resulting project: CH01 P1 degrees0/0/0/1; Note defaultX; step 13NoteX/Vel 50; Vel 80/Len1/2 defaults retained. CH02 unchanged. Applied C major restored.

2. Open Merge modes. Compare Skip and All for Trig.
3. Play and stop after each comparison.
4. Unassign pattern 2 from CH01 before continuing.

title: Combining Pattern Overlaps
summary: Trig, note, velocity and length merge choices are independent.
prose:
1. Assign two patterns to a channel.
2. Open Channel tasks → Merge modes.
3. Select Strategy with E2.
4. Choose Skip, Only or All with E3 and compare playback. The choice requests immediately; no K3 Apply is required. Active shows the sounding strategy; Pending names an accepted change waiting for its boundary.
5. Select the note, velocity or length merge row with E2 and edit its value with E3.

Skip removes overlapping attacks. All retains attacks from either pattern. Only retains shared attacks. Foundation and Fragments are alternative choices of this same Strategy selector, not additional modes layered over Skip, Only or All. Foundation controls trigs while note, velocity and length merge settings remain active. Fragments controls all four attributes; retained note, velocity and length settings are inactive until a strategy that uses them becomes active.

Skip is the default Strategy.

Example: channel 1 plays pattern 1 with trigs on steps 1 to 4 (C, D, E, F: MIDI 60, 62, 64, 65). Pattern 2 has trigs on steps 1 and 2. Assign both to the channel, open Channel tasks > Merge modes and compare:

* Skip: steps 3 and 4 play (MIDI 64, 65). Steps 1 and 2 are in both patterns and drop out.
* Only: steps 1 and 2 play. Steps 3 and 4 drop out.
* All: all four steps play (MIDI 60, 62, 64, 65).

Then select Note mode and compare AVERAGE with PAT 2: with PAT 2 every step takes pattern 2’s note, so the same rhythm plays on one pitch.

recipes.title: Make one step override a channel Note default, then restore inheritance
recipes.text:
1. On Masks, set the channel Note default to G3.
2. Hold step 1 and set its Note to C4; release the step and check that the channel readout returns to G3 while step 1 keeps its exception.
3. Add a D4 exception on step 2, then clear step 1 and finally clear all step exceptions with K1+K2.

recipes.title: Contrast inherited velocity with explicit zero and a cleared exception
recipes.text:
1. Set the channel Vel mask to 50 and add a step-1 accent at 90.
2. Hold step 2 and set Vel to 0; read zero while held, then release and inspect the phrase with step 2 silent.
3. Hold step 2, press K2 and release it; the step inherits 50 again while the step-1 accent remains.
Outcome: X inherits the channel velocity; an explicit 0 silences the step. Clearing the step mask restores 50 without erasing the 90 accent.

Hold a step and turn E3 to lock a different value on that step only; hold the step and press K2 to clear its lock. 2. Tap Channel (3,8).

4. Return to Song and select slot 2 at (2,1).

5. In Slot setup select Song mode, set On and press K3 to apply.

Bass alone → bass and phrase → bass alone → bass and phrase. The highlighted Song slot changes at each boundary.

title: Dig Deeper
summary: Reference sections for pattern editing, channel processing and song arrangement.
prose:
Use the following reference sections to edit patterns, process channels and arrange song sequences. Work in this order:

1. Pattern Editor: create source patterns. Adding Trigs sets when a pattern plays, Adding Notes which scale degree, Adding Velocity how hard.
2. Channel Editor: assign a device and patterns to each channel, then shape the result with masks, merge modes, clocks and trig params.
3. Scale Editor: choose the scales and degrees the notes are read against.
4. Song Editor: copy finished sequences into Song slots and arrange them.

title: Pattern Editor
summary: Edit source-pattern trigs, scale-relative notes and velocities, then assign the patterns to channels.
prose:
Patterns are the building blocks of your harmony and rhythm sections. Create source patterns in the pattern editors, assign them to channels, then use channel merging to combine or remix their trig, note and velocity data.

Press Pattern, grid (5,8), the third button of the global menu cluster, to open the Pattern Editor. Press it again to move through its three pages: Pattern Trig (which steps play), Pattern Note (which scale degree each step plays) and Pattern Velocity (how hard). The top row, (1,1) to (16,1), selects which of the 16 patterns you edit. Each pattern has 64 steps. Pattern Trig shows all 64 on grid rows 4 to 7, 16 per row. Pattern Note and Pattern Velocity show 16 steps at a time and the buttons at (9,8) to (12,8) choose steps 1–16, 17–32, 33–48 or 49–64.

Watch: [Pattern editor demo](https://youtu.be/J1ckUZvhFJ0?t=660)

title: Adding Trigs
summary: Enter pattern trigs manually or preview and paint a generated rhythm.
prose:
Trigs are added in the pattern editor. Using the top row, pick one of the 16 available patterns.

Press a sequencer step to enter a trig. Active trigs glow brightly. Hold a trig and select its end step to set its length. Dimmer steps show the note’s duration. Another trig in the same pattern ends that duration.

Select a built-in rhythm algorithm using the five algorithm buttons. From left to right:

* Button 1: The drum algorithm, using banks of classic drum patterns.
* Button 2: The tresillo algorithm, utilizing a 3/3/2 ratio for diverse rhythm variations. The tresillo multiplier can be set on the Norns screen for more variations.
* Button 3: Euclidean, a rhythm tool rooted in mathematical logic.
* Button 4: NE Numeric Repetitor, another rhythm tool based on mathematical principles.
* Button 5: Rhythm Doctor, a capture and paint workflow described below. Recording needs the sequencer stopped; an analysed bank can be used while it plays.

Pressing an algorithm button shows the Trig Algorithm screen on the norns, with the algorithm in use marked SELECTED. You can also choose there: E2 moves through the five algorithms and K3 selects one, exactly as its grid button does. Choosing Rhythm Doctor opens the Doctor. Algorithm, in the pattern task list, opens the same screen.

Use the row-3 bank fader starting at column 12 to choose a bank: five choices for Drum and Tresillo, four for Numeric Repetitor. Euclidean and Rhythm Doctor do not use this selector.

Use the left fader in row 2 for the first algorithm parameter and the left fader in row 3 for the second. The two end buttons are brightly lit and change the value by one: the far-left button steps down and the far-right button steps up. The dimmer buttons between them choose broader proportional values, with the centre selecting the middle value. The second fader is disabled for Drum, and both are disabled for Rhythm Doctor. Changing an enabled parameter refreshes the prepared pattern; use Paint to commit it.

Press a grid control to display its function on the norns.

### Previewing and painting

Press Prime to preview the selected algorithm’s pattern. Potential new steps are shown as flashing bright steps on the sequencer. While these steps flash, they are not painted yet. Any step that would be painted over an existing active step blinks dimly. By painting the new pattern, you deactivate the faintly blinking steps. You can modify algorithm parameters while the pattern is primed.

If you have not painted the new pattern, the prime button continues to blink. Pressing it again paints your edits. Pressing the prime button again without tweaking the algorithm or its parameters acts as an undo for the last action.

Press Cancel to discard a prepared pattern.

While previewing a new pattern, use the move controls to shift its position. The first button shifts it left, the third shifts it right and the centre button resets it. Press the same rightmost control at (16,8) again to commit the changes. This manual calls its preview-start action Prime and its commit action Paint; both use the same grid key. Pressing prime, cancel or a move button shows the Paint Preview screen on the norns: whether a preview is showing, the algorithm it comes from, the shift, and how many steps it triggers. In Rhythm Doctor these same three buttons browse the recording instead (see Rhythm Doctor).

On the norns screen, Pattern Trig shows the pattern you are editing brightly over the viewed channel’s steps, which stay dim as context; the viewed channel is the merged version of the channel. The title row names both (`PAT02 CH01`). Channel view, in the Pattern tasks list, shows the viewed channel on its own. Use E3 to view another channel; it does not change the selected channel. Choose Options from Pattern tasks (E1) to edit the tresillo multiplier in use; a new multiplier takes effect the next time you prime the tresillo algorithm. Change the multiplier and prime Tresillo again to compare the generated rhythm.

Pattern tasks, opened with E1, lists Pattern, Options, Algorithm, Channel view and, while the Rhythm Doctor algorithm is chosen, Rhythm Doctor.

Watch: [Pattern editor trig page demo](https://youtu.be/J1ckUZvhFJ0?t=668)

details.title: Algorithm faders
details.text: Use the left faders to edit the generated pattern before painting. The first fader occupies columns 1–10 of row 2; the second occupies the same columns of row 3. Each end button, lit more brightly than the rest, changes its value by one (left steps down, right steps up). The dimmer inner buttons select proportional values, with the centre selecting the middle value. The enabled parameters depend on the algorithm: Drum uses Pattern 1 (1–128); Tresillo uses Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 (each 1–128); Euclidean uses Fill and Length (each 1–32); Numeric Repetitor uses Pattern 1 (1–32) and Pattern 2 (1–16). Rhythm Doctor disables these faders and uses its capture controls.

details.title: Bank selection
details.text: Select banks with the row-3 fader starting at column 12. Drum and Tresillo have five bank choices; Numeric Repetitor has four. Euclidean and Rhythm Doctor do not use bank selection. Changing an enabled parameter or bank refreshes the prepared algorithm pattern.

details.title: Trig options
details.text: Use E1 to open Pattern tasks, select Options with E2, and press K3. E3 saves the Tresillo amount immediately; K3 has no apply action on this page. Change the amount, then prime Tresillo again on the grid to regenerate its preview. Painting the preview commits it to the selected pattern.

recipes.title: Preview a shifted Numeric pattern, cancel it, then commit a fresh preview
recipes.text:
Starting point: use a new empty project with playback stopped and Record Off. Select Pattern 1 on channel 1. The [Move a rhythm before committing](#adding-trigs/paint-shift-and-cancel) capture starts with 8 flashing trigs at Shift 0 (steps 5, 13, 21, 29 and onward). Its controls are Prime (16,8), Move right (12,8) and Cancel (14,8). The captured result is replayed by the manual; on hardware, the preview uses the selected Numeric settings.

1. Select Numeric Repetitor at (15,2) and press Prime (16,8). Check the Preview readout: Algorithm Numeric, Shift 0 and 8 trigs.

2. Tap Move right (12,8) once. The flashing steps shift one step to the right, starting at step 6; the readout is Shift +1.

3. Tap Cancel (14,8). Check Preview OFF and Trigs NONE; the pattern has not been painted.

4. Press Prime (16,8) again, tap Move right (12,8) once and press Prime again to commit. The new pattern stays one step to the right; only this committed preview is painted.

Outcome: Cancel discards the preview without writing trigs. A fresh shifted preview can be committed; the captured result shows the preview state, while the project changes only after the final Prime.

title: Rhythm Doctor
summary: Select the fifth pattern algorithm at grid column 16, row 2 to capture, analyse and paint rhythm lanes.
prose:
Rhythm Doctor is the fifth pattern-editor algorithm, at grid column 16, row 2.
Setup and workflow screens use labelled vertical rows. E2 selects an editable row and E3 changes it. The contextual footer names confirmation actions; painting still uses the grid Paint control.
Each project retains one captured bank. Select a lane, preview a 64-step
window, then paint it into the selected pattern.

### Record and paint a phrase

Use Rhythm Doctor to turn a rhythm you can play into the norns audio input, such as a drum loop, into a Mosaic pattern. Before you start, stop the sequencer, assign a device and a pattern to the channel you will paint into, and have the source ready to play. In the example captured below the source is a steady 120 BPM test loop with one thump on every beat.

1. Press Pattern (5,8) and select the Rhythm Doctor algorithm at (16,2). The norns shows RHYTHM DR with Record READY, Tempo AUTO, Manual BPM and Input STEREO.
2. Optional: turn E2 to Tempo and E3 to MANUAL, set Manual BPM, and press K3 to confirm. Leave Tempo on AUTO to let Doctor estimate it.
3. Tap Record at (1,2) and play the audio. The screen shows CAPTURE and MORE AUDIO NEEDED, then ENOUGH / REC OR K3.
4. Press K3 to finish. The screen shows ANALYSING and the lanes BD, SD and CYM.
5. When the Window screen reads READY, select a lane: BD at (3,2), SD at (4,2) or CYM at (5,2).
6. Select the destination pattern on the top row and tap Paint at (16,8). Detected hits flash on the grid as a preview. Tap Paint again to commit; the tooltip reads Pattern painted. Cancel at (14,8) discards the preview.
7. Press Channel (3,8) and Play (1,8) to hear the painted rhythm.

With the 120 BPM test loop, BD paints a hit on every fourth step.

Recording needs the sequencer stopped, because capture takes over the audio
input and analysis replaces the bank underneath whatever is on the screen. So
does Alignment, which re-analyses. Record, capture setup and Alignment do
nothing while the sequencer runs, and the screen says `STOP SEQUENCER` when
there is no bank to work on instead.

A bank that has already been analysed stays usable while the sequencer plays.
Choosing a lane, browsing the recording, changing sensitivity or paint policy,
and previewing and painting all read a finished bank and write to a pattern,
which is what the rest of the Trigger Editor already lets you do while playing.
Starting the sequencer cancels an unfinished capture or analysis and closes a
capture-setup or alignment draft, but keeps an armed paint preview, so you can
arm Paint, start the sequencer and commit. Rhythm Doctor does not start or stop
the sequencer for you.

On an empty bank, press grid column 1, row 2 to begin Record; the press starts
the action and its release is consumed. Press Record again to stop, or press K3:
either finishes the capture once the screen says `ENOUGH / REC OR K3`. Until it
does, the screen says `MORE AUDIO NEEDED`, and pressing Record then asks whether
to abandon the take instead. Pressing Record on an occupied bank asks whether to
clear its capture bank. K2 cancels that question and K3 confirms it; clearing keeps patterns that
were already painted. In a ready bank, use E2 to choose Window bar, Window
step, selected-lane sensitivity, Paint policy, or Alignment, then use E3 to
edit the chosen item. Window bar moves by 16 steps and Window step by one; both
view the same bounded timeline. Alignment shows `OPEN >`: choose it and press
K3 (or turn E3) to open its tempo, start-beat, and fine-start settings; K2
cancels and K3 applies the draft.

Before recording, use E2/E3 to open and edit the setup draft for Auto or Manual tempo, manual BPM (40–240), and Stereo/L/R input. Press K3 to confirm the settings for the take, or K2 to discard the draft. Record uses the confirmed settings.

Stereo records left and right separately. L records the left input into both recorded channels; R records the right input into both. Auto estimates tempo and phrase start from the recording. Manual uses the selected integer BPM and starts the phrase at the beginning of recording. Applying an explicit Alignment draft later replaces that capture timing.

To paint a ready lane, select the destination pattern with the top row, press
Paint (column 16, row 8) to preview, then press it again to commit. Cancel
(column 14, row 8) discards the preview. Toggle is the default paint policy;
Add and Replace are selectable on the Rhythm Doctor screen. Painting does not
alter the captured bank.

Prime, Cancel and the preview-shift buttons work the same way in every algorithm; see Adding Trigs. In Rhythm Doctor the buttons at (10,8), (11,8) and (12,8) browse the recording instead (see Finding the phrase below).

Watch: [Pattern editor trig page demo](https://youtu.be/J1ckUZvhFJ0?t=668)

### Set up the analysis server

## Prerequisites

Install [Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads/) and [Python](https://www.python.org/downloads/) on the computer that will run the server. The Windows steps below were checked on Windows 10/11 with Python 3.10. On Linux or macOS, use an installed Python 3.9 or newer.

Get the Mosaic checkout and enter the server folder:

```sh
git clone --branch codex/1.4.0 https://github.com/subvertnormality/mosaic.git
cd mosaic
cd tools/rhythm_doctor_server
```

## Install the server

Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
py -3.10 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt pyyaml
```

Linux or macOS:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt pyyaml
```

Demucs and Beat This fetch and cache their model weights when first used. Let that first model load finish before analysing a capture.

The server provides six lanes without LarsNet: `DRUMS`, `BASS`, `GUITAR`, `PIANO`, `VOCALS` and `OTHER`. To keep six lanes, skip the optional LarsNet commands below and leave `LARSNET_ROOT` unset. To split the kit into ten lanes, install LarsNet as well. Its checkpoint archive is about 562 MB and is licensed CC BY-NC 4.0; read that licence before using it, especially for commercial work. The following commands fetch the published archive and verify its SHA-256.

Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/polimi-ispl/larsnet .\larsnet
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install gdown
.\.venv\Scripts\python fetch_models.py --larsnet-root .\larsnet --sha256 dd785d77f66413c5acbd3a4cedac02951578c838496d059930c43f159647c907
$env:LARSNET_ROOT = "$PWD\larsnet"
```

Linux or macOS:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/polimi-ispl/larsnet ./larsnet
.venv/bin/python -m pip install gdown
.venv/bin/python fetch_models.py --larsnet-root ./larsnet --sha256 dd785d77f66413c5acbd3a4cedac02951578c838496d059930c43f159647c907
export LARSNET_ROOT="$PWD/larsnet"
```

## Start and check the server

From `tools/rhythm_doctor_server`, start it on all network interfaces at port 8420:

Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python server.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8420
```

Linux or macOS:

```sh
.venv/bin/python server.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8420
```

On Windows, allow the firewall prompt on private networks. The startup log should report `ready=True`. On the computer, open `http://127.0.0.1:8420/v1/health` in a browser; the response should contain `"ready": true` and a lane list. Only read the lane count when `ready` is true: ten lanes means LarsNet loaded, six means it did not. If required Demucs or Beat This models are missing, the server normally exits. The diagnostic option `--allow-missing-models` keeps it running with `ready:false`; analysis is unavailable in that state. Keep the terminal and server running while using Rhythm Doctor; press Ctrl+C in that terminal to stop it.

## Connect Mosaic on norns

Find the computer’s IPv4 address with `ipconfig` on Windows, or the network settings on Linux/macOS. If the norns is providing the access point, use the computer address on its `10.42.0.x` subnet. Otherwise use the address on the same network as the norns. In `PARAMS > MOSAIC > Rhythm Doctor`, set **Analysis server** to the computer’s reachable address, such as `http://192.168.1.50:8420`, and turn **Use analysis server** on. Enter the reachable computer address, not `0.0.0.0` or `127.0.0.1`.

If the server is enabled and reachable, a successful capture uses its six or ten lanes. Turn **Use analysis server** off to keep its address saved and use on-device analysis. If the remote request fails, Mosaic falls back only if its local analysis backend is available; otherwise it reports `ANALYSIS_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` and creates no bank. If you see only `BD`, `SD` and `CYM`, check the switch, address, health response, network and firewall.

Beat This estimates tempo and phrase start from the mix before separation. Treat them as estimates and adjust Alignment when needed.

details.title: Lanes
details.text:
The lanes occupy a block of five columns on each of two rows, starting at
column 3: lanes one to five on row 2 at columns 3–7, and lanes six to ten on
row 3 at the same columns. Column 1 of row 2 is Record, column 2 is reserved,
and columns 12–16 of both rows belong to the algorithm and bank-mask faders and
are never lanes. A bank analysed on the device declares three lanes — **BD**
(bass drum), **SD** (snare drum) and **CYM** (hi-hats and cymbals) — so only
the first three cells light. A remote analysis declares up to ten, which is why
the block is two rows: a single row would run the later lanes under the
algorithm fader, where selecting one would also change the algorithm.

Lanes read in kit order rather than alphabetically: kick, snare, hi-hat,
cymbals and toms fill the top row, and whatever else the analysis separated out
— bass, guitar, piano, vocals and demucs' residual **OTHER** — follows on the
bottom row. A lane neither of those names keeps a stable alphabetical place
after the ones they do, so an unfamiliar backend still puts its columns in the
same order every time a project loads. A bank saved before this order existed
is brought forward when it loads, so an older capture does not keep an
alphabetical grid until it is recorded again.

The lanes describe what can be told apart reliably, not a full drum-kit
transcription. **CYM** is hats *and* cymbals together because a closed hat and a
ride are both inharmonic metal with overlapping spectra, and the decay that
distinguishes them in isolation is buried in a mix; separating them was measured
and does not work. Bass, open hi-hat and tom have no lane: none could be
detected reliably enough to paint. Bass was tried and withdrawn — every
approach either failed to separate a bass note from the kick that hides it, or
marked the kicks themselves, so the lane only ever restated what BD already
said.

details.title: Finding the phrase and Alignment
details.text:
**Finding the phrase.** Auto estimates where the four-bar phrase begins and aligns gates to it. Manual starts the phrase at the beginning of recording; Alignment can move it afterward. In this mode columns 10, 11 and 12 of row 8 browse the recording, and
they do it with the same gestures that shift a previewed pattern everywhere
else. A press of column 10 or 12 moves the window one step back or forward.
Holding either of them covers a whole four-bar phrase in that direction, which
is exactly the width of the displayed window, so every position reached by
holding stays aligned with the phrase. A press of column 11 returns to the
calculated phrase start. E3 still moves by a single bar or step. In every
other algorithm those three buttons continue to shift a previewed pattern's
position.

Each move names where it landed, as bar.beat.step, so the tooltip
identifies the current window position. A move that the
recording absorbs -- a step forward when the window is already at the last
whole phrase, or a return to a phrase start you are already sitting on --
says so instead of reporting a move that did not happen. If you are painting
while you browse, the preview follows the window: the grid keeps showing the
gates under the part of the recording you are looking at.

In Auto, use the estimated phrase start as an initial position. A crash on the first beat or a fill before the bar provides evidence for the boundary. Identical bars can make it undecidable; check the reported confidence.

Open Alignment to change Start beat. Auto browses the detected beat grid. Manual browses a regular beat grid spaced by the confirmed BPM from the confirmed phrase origin. The Manual grid covers the retained recording, including earlier beats before a later chosen phrase origin; choices stay inside the recording.

Turn E2 to select Start beat and E3 to choose another beat. Press K3 to apply: Mosaic reanalyses the same retained recording using that phrase origin. No new recording is needed. Confirming without changing the beat preserves its position. Changing Exact BPM and applying rebuilds the regular beat spacing at the confirmed tempo. K2 cancels the draft and leaves the bank unchanged.

A reloaded bank can still be browsed and painted, but alignment correction needs the retained capture audio. If that audio is unavailable, K3 refuses with CAPTURE AUDIO UNAVAILABLE instead of changing the bank.

details.title: Analysis server (advanced)
details.text: **Optional computer analysis server.** Rhythm Doctor analyses on the norns by default. To add six or ten remote lanes, follow “Set up the analysis server” in the instructions above. Remote analysis needs a reachable computer; the local three-lane analysis remains the fallback when available.

details.title: Local analysis and availability
details.text:
**Availability:** Rhythm Doctor analyses captures on norns by default. The first
capture may take about half a minute while local analysis starts; a 45-second
capture also takes about half a minute to analyse. If local analysis fails,
Mosaic reports `ANALYSIS_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` and does not create a bank. See
**If local analysis fails** for the norns setup needed to retry.

details.title: Recording and playback
details.text: Stop the transport before recording. After analysis produces a ready bank, browse, adjust and paint it while playback runs.

details.title: Capture and analysis results
details.text: Capture, analysis and painting are separate stages. A backend failure shows an explicit error and does not produce a ready bank. The ten broad instrument lanes of the optional analysis server are experimental; no detection accuracy is specified.

details.title: Paint destination
details.text: Select the destination pattern and song slot before previewing. Changing either invalidates the prepared Doctor paint preview. Preview again before committing.

details.title: If local analysis fails
details.text: Local analysis requires Python 3 and gcc (a C compiler) on norns. If either is missing or the analysis build fails, install or restore the dependency and try again. Mosaic reports `ANALYSIS_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` and does not create a bank until analysis succeeds. No third-party Python packages or network download are required.

details.title: Vertical list controls
details.text: Rhythm Doctor’s setup, capture, analysis, window, alignment and paint screens show labelled vertical rows. Select an editable row with E2 and change it with E3. Read the contextual footer before confirming an action: the grid Paint button remains the painting control, and K3 does not substitute for it. This display change does not change capture, lane selection or paint scope.

details.title: Confirmed capture setup
details.text: Confirm the setup with K3 before Record. Stereo preserves separate left/right channels; L or R duplicates that chosen input into both channels. Manual uses 40–240 integer BPM from recording start; Auto estimates tempo and phrase start. A later explicitly confirmed Alignment draft takes precedence.

details.title: Start beat and retained recording
details.text: Manual Start beat follows a regular grid at the confirmed BPM and phrase origin, including earlier beats when they are inside the recording. Auto uses detected beats. Apply reanalyses the retained recording; Exact BPM correction rebuilds regular beat spacing. After reload, a usable bank may lack original audio: K3 reports CAPTURE AUDIO UNAVAILABLE and leaves it unchanged. K2 cancels without changing the bank.

title: Adding Notes
summary: Set source-pattern notes as scale degrees relative to the channel’s active root.
prose:
Pattern notes are positions relative to the active scale root, not fixed pitches. In C major, position 0 is C, one step above is D and one step below is B. Changing the channel scale to E minor makes the same positions E, F sharp and D.

Sequenced scale and degree changes described in [Harmony Design](#harmony-design) affect pattern output. Use pattern notes for harmony and rhythm parts. Patterns can also provide melodies, but changing a scale progression changes their tonality. Use [Masks](#masks) to enter a deliberate melody independently.

From Pattern Trig, press the third global-menu button again to open Pattern Note.

The grid displays 16 steps at a time. Active trigs show dim vertical bars; a dim horizontal line marks the root. Selected note values glow brightly. Press a cell in a step’s column to set its note. Hold K1 while entering a note to copy it to the corresponding position across all four step pages.

The channel supplies the scale; the pattern does not own it. The same source pattern can therefore play different notes on different channels. Think of patterns as disconnected from channels: this is why Mosaic is an intentioned generative sequencer, so expect happy accidents. Use the norns channel grid viewer to inspect channel output.

Use the step-page buttons to select one of four groups of 16 steps.

Use the outer note-range buttons to move the displayed range up or down one step. Hold an outer button to reach its extreme. Press the middle button to return to the page with the root note on the bottom row.

A step without a trig can still store note data for use by another merge mode.

The top row flickers to indicate the selected pattern. Hold a top-row button, or hold K1 and press it, to select another pattern.

The norns Pattern Note screen shows the viewed channel’s steps as 64 cells. Turn E3 to view another channel.

### Enter a rising line

1. In Pattern Trig, tap steps 1 to 4 on grid row 4: (1,4), (2,4), (3,4) and (4,4).
2. Press Pattern (5,8) to open Pattern Note.
3. Tap (1,7), (2,6), (3,5) and (4,4). Row 7 is the root and each row above it is one scale degree higher, so these are degrees 0, 1, 2 and 3.
4. With the pattern assigned to a channel in C major, press Play (1,8). The line is C, D, E, F: MIDI 60, 62, 64, 65.

Hold K1 while you tap to write the same note on all four step pages.

### Reach other octaves

The seven rows are one window onto the scale. In C major with the root page showing, (4,7) is MIDI 60 and (4,1) is MIDI 71. Tap range-up at (14,8) to move the window up one scale degree: (4,1) becomes 72. Tap range-down at (16,8) to move it down one degree. Hold range-up to jump to the highest window, where (4,1) is MIDI 83, or hold range-down to jump to the lowest window, where (4,7) is MIDI 48. Tap the centre button at (15,8) to return to the root page.

Watch: [Pattern editor note page demo](https://youtu.be/J1ckUZvhFJ0?t=1121)

details.title: Source notes and channel pitch
details.text: The pattern stores distance from a scale root. Each channel applies its active scale and subsequent processing. An edit affects every channel using that source pattern. A step without a source trig can supply note data when a different pattern supplies the merged rhythm.

title: Adding Velocity
summary: Set source-pattern velocities using fourteen discrete grid levels from MIDI 127 to 0.
prose:
From Pattern Note, press the third global-menu button again to open Pattern Velocity.

The velocity editor operates like the note editor. Its two extreme vertical pages show velocities 127–68 and 58–0. Press a velocity-range button to move the displayed range by one value level. Hold it to reach an extreme.

The norns Pattern Velocity screen shows the viewed channel’s steps as 64 cells. Turn E3 to view another channel.

### Set an accent and a rest

1. Press Pattern (5,8) until Pattern Velocity opens.
2. Each step’s column is a seven-level fader. On the first page, from the top row down, (x,1) is 127, (x,2) is 117, (x,3) is 107, (x,4) is 97, (x,5) is 87, (x,6) is 78 and (x,7) is 68. Tap (4,1) for an accent on step 4, or (4,7) for a soft hit.
3. To silence a step, hold (16,8). The window jumps to the lower page, 58 at the top down to 0 at the bottom. Tap (4,7) to set velocity 0.
4. Hold (15,8) to return to the upper page.

A step at velocity 0 sends no note: it is a rest. Hold K1 while you tap to write the same level on all four step pages.

Watch: [Pattern editor velocity page demo](https://youtu.be/J1ckUZvhFJ0?t=1229)

details.title: Grid levels are discrete
details.text: Fourteen source levels span MIDI 127 to 0. The initial seven levels are 127, 117, 107, 97, 87, 78 and 68; the lower extreme shows 58, 48, 39, 29, 19, 9 and 0. A short range-button press moves the seven-row window by one level rather than adjusting MIDI velocity by one. The window stops at both extremes.

title: Channel Editor
summary: Select one of 16 channels and open its editing tasks.
prose:
Press the far-left global menu button to open Channel Editor. Press a button in the top channel-select row to select one of the 16 channels.

[Channel editor demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J1ckUZvhFJ0&t=1357s)

The scale-slot row displays the selected channel’s active scale slot while playback runs. Holding a step with a scale lock shows its locked slot.

Use the five octave buttons in grid row 8, columns 8–12, to set the selected channel’s offset from −2 to +2 octaves. Press the centre button, column 10, for zero offset. Hold a step and choose an octave to set a step override. Press the same explicit octave again to remove its lock.

details.title: Scale-slot feedback
details.text: The scale-slot row indicates the selected channel’s active scale slot during playback. When a step with a scale lock is held, the row displays that lock instead of the moving active-scale indicator.

details.title: Channel octave scope
details.text: The octave fader applies to the selected channel, not every channel in the pattern. Its centre sets a zero-octave offset; it does not disable a separate global-octave setting. Hold a step and choose an octave to set its override. Choosing the same explicit step octave again removes that lock; otherwise the channel offset applies.

recipes.title: Return from a held-step edit to the page you were using
recipes.text:
Starting point: playback is stopped, channel 3 is selected and its Masks page is open. No step is held and Note reads X. This example separates a step-only edit from inspecting a step while another Channel task is open.

1. Hold step 5 at grid (5,4). The header reads NOTE MASKS CH03 ST05. Turn E2 anticlockwise until Note is selected, then turn E3 clockwise one detent. The step Note changes from X to C-2 (MIDI 0), the lowest note value. A Note mask alone does not create a trig.
2. Release step 5. The header returns to NOTE MASKS CH03 and the channel Note still reads X: the C-2 exception belongs only to step 5.
3. Turn E1 until Channel tasks opens. Turn E2 to Clock and press K3. Check the Clock page for CH03.
4. Hold step 9 at grid (9,4). The screen temporarily shows NOTE MASKS CH03 ST09. Do not hold step 5 or change a value during this separate inspection.
5. Release step 9. Clock returns, because it was the page you were using before the hold.

Use a step hold to inspect or edit one exception without losing your place in another Channel task. The earlier step-5 edit and the later step-9 inspection are separate gestures.

title: Devices
summary: Assign an output device to the selected channel.
prose:
Assign a device to a channel before sending notes. A device represents a hardware instrument, software running on a computer, or a sound source within norns.

[Devices demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J1ckUZvhFJ0&t=1358s)

title: MIDI Sound Sources
summary: Route a channel to a configured MIDI output, device and MIDI channel.
prose:
Select either an internal norns sound engine supplied by [n.b.](https://github.com/sixolet/nb/tree/main) or a MIDI device in the workspace. Devices are assigned per scene and retain their settings across all song sequences. Configure a MIDI output device in norns before selecting a MIDI sound source.

If a device configuration file is available, such as a configuration for an Elektron -takt instrument, select the device by name and edit its labelled parameters. If no configuration is available, select the CC device and enter MIDI CC numbers from the receiving instrument’s documentation.

title: Norns Sound Sources with n.b.
summary: Select an installed supported n.b. voice for internal audio or Crow output.
prose:
Install a supported [n.b.](https://github.com/sixolet/nb/tree/main) mod to sequence internal sound sources or devices connected through Crow. Supported mods include:

* [nb_ansible](https://github.com/sixolet/nb_ansible) for Ansible voices.
* [emplaitress](https://github.com/sixolet/emplaitress/) offers four MI Plaits voices in parallel. Emplaitress's params can be locked in _Mosaic_. Emplaitress is sensitive to rapid notes. Check playback when using arpeggios, chords or small clock divisions.
* [nb_jf](https://github.com/sixolet/nb_jf) accesses multiple voice modes from Just Friends, including individual mono voice (with slew), polysynth, kit, and unison modes.
* [nb_crow](https://github.com/sixolet/nb_crow) for Crow v/8 and envelope functions.
* [nb_drum_crow](https://github.com/entzmingerc/nb_drumcrow) turns a monome crow into a synthesizer.
* [nb_polyperc](https://github.com/dstroud/nb_polyperc) poly perc. Poly perc's params can be locked in _Mosaic_.
* [nb_rudiments](https://github.com/entzmingerc/nb_rudiments) percussion synth.
* [nb_doubledecker](https://github.com/sixolet/doubledecker) 2-layer synth. Doubledecker's params can be locked in _Mosaic_.
* [nb_oilcan](https://github.com/zjb-s/oilcan) percussion sync. Oilcan's params can be locked in _Mosaic_.

For [nb_polyperc](https://github.com/dstroud/nb_polyperc), install it through the [Maiden Project Manager](https://monome.org/docs/norns/maiden/), or run `;install https://github.com/dstroud/nb_polyperc` in the Maiden REPL. Restart norns with `SYSTEM > RESTART` so the installed mod is discovered. Then open `SYSTEM > MODS`, select `nb_polyperc` with E2 and enable it with E3. Restart norns again; Mosaic can then offer Polyperc 1 in the Device picker. One Polyperc voice is enabled by default. To add voices, open `SYSTEM > MODS > NB_POLYPERC` from the K1 menu, press K3 to open the mod menu and adjust E3. See the [norns mod guide](https://monome.org/docs/norns/mods/) for the install, enable and restart sequence. Adding too many internal sound engines to channels can overload norns.

details.title: Choose three voices for a phrase
details.text: Open Channel tasks, select Device and turn E3 to choose an installed voice. In the example, assign Oilcan 1 to channel 1, Polyperc 1 to channel 2 and Doubledecker to channel 3. Press K3 to apply each selection, then listen to the linked three-voice example to hear the result.

title: Device Parameters
summary: Store MIDI parameter values and transmit them when loading Mosaic or starting playback.
prose:
Use the norns params menu to store a MIDI device’s patch parameters. All CC parameters defined by its configuration are available for editing. Set a parameter to its configured Off value (default -1) to leave the receiving device’s current value unchanged. Any other value sends that MIDI value to the device.

Loading Mosaic or starting playback transmits the stored enabled MIDI parameter values. The values remain consistent across song patterns, preserving sound settings within the Mosaic patch. Use patch recall for devices with limited MIDI parameters or difficult parameter interfaces.

NRPN encoding is explicit: new generic configurations use standard 14-bit values, while existing projects preserve their historical output. See [NRPN encoding and project conversion](docs/testing/NRPN_COMPATIBILITY.md) for device settings and deliberate conversion without rewriting numeric values.

[Devices parameters demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J1ckUZvhFJ0&t=1454s)

details.title: Stored value and step lock
details.text: The stored value is the one in the norns params; a step lock set in Trig params only applies to that step. Locking step 1 of CC 1 to 99 sends 99 before that step's note, while the stored 63 is used on the other steps and still reads 63 afterwards.

details.title: Off reads X
details.text: In the params menu an Off parameter reads X. This is the configured Off value (default -1) and nothing is sent for it.

details.title: Which example to read
details.text: The examples below run in this order. Move between parameter locks and Slide only one source lock show a parameter ramping between two locked steps, first for every source and then for one. Set a configured device parameter shows the values a configured control accepts, from 0 up to its 127 limit. Keep a stored value while locking a step shows the stored value and a step lock together.

recipes.title: Shape a CC ramp between two step locks
recipes.text:
Starting point: channel 1 is routed to the example MIDI device and its active phrase has steps 1–4.

1. In PARAMS > MOSAIC, set the device’s Control 1 to 63, then return to Mosaic. Open Channel tasks with E1, choose Trig params with E2 and press K3.
2. Select slot 1 with E2, press K2 to open its assignment list, turn E3 to CC 1, press K3 to assign it, then press K2 to return. The slot reads the stored 63.
3. Hold step 1 at (1,4), turn E3 anticlockwise to 24 and release. Hold step 3 at (3,4), turn E3 clockwise to 96 and release. Hold step 4 at (4,4), turn E3 anticlockwise to 48 and release.
4. Hold step 1 again and press K3, then release. The slide belongs to that step. Pressing K3 with no step held would instead toggle the channel-wide slide.
5. Tap Play at (1,8), let two loops run, then stop. CC 1 glides from 24 toward 96, followed by the direct jump to 48 at step 4.
6. Reopen PARAMS > MOSAIC and inspect Control 1: the stored value remains 63.

Outcome: the local slide shapes the emitted controller values without overwriting the stored device value.

recipes.title: Compare a stored device value with one step-local CC lock
recipes.text:
Start with channel 1 routed to the generic CC Device and a four-trig phrase on pattern 1, steps 1–4. This comparison changes the sequenced messages while keeping the instrument’s stored starting value.

1. Tap K1, open PARAMS → MOSAIC and store device CC 1 at 63. Return to Mosaic.
2. Open Channel tasks → Trig params. Select slot 1 with E2, press K2, browse to CC 1 with E3, press K3 to assign it and K2 to return. The slot reads 63.
3. Hold step 1 at (1,4), turn E3 to 99 and release. Play and stop: step 1 sends CC 1 = 99; unmodified steps send 63.
